To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the fastigial nucleus is involved in saccade-related activity.

(i) the saccade-related activity of the fastigial nucleus is modulated by eye position; (ii) the activity of a population of FOR neurons is related to eye velocity; (iii) FOR neurons are not sensitive to the direction of the eye velocity.
saccade related activity of FN neurones is not eye position dependent and that the activity is related to saccade metrics.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following questions: (1) Do saccade-related burst patterns of single units in the caudal fastgial nucleus reflect the saccade metrics?
the analysis of the activity of single FOR neurones, with the aim of understanding the mechanisms of their contribution to saccade control.
the role of the cerebellar oculomotor structures in the control of saccades.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the fastigial nucleus is involved in the generation of horizontal saccades, and that it does this by providing an input to the brainstem oculomotor system that is independent of the position of the eye.
saccade metrics are affected by the FOR, but the precise mechanisms by which this is achieved are still unclear.
FOR neurones are not eye-position dependent, but they are saccade-related, and that their activity is related to saccade duration and direction.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the fastigial oculoromotor region, FN (fastigiual oculomotor area, FOA), plays a role in the control of saccade metrics, but not in the control of the eye position.
FOR neurones do not code for eye position, but that they are involved in the control of saccades by means of a time-dependent modulation of their firing activity.
we found that the discharge of FOR neurones depends on eye position, but only for the contralateral eye.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the activity of a population of FOR neurons can be decomposed into two distinct components: (i) a burst that is triggered by a saccade and is independent of eye position, and (ii) a tonic component that increases with eye position.
FOR neurones do not act without receiving information on eye position.
saccade control involves a large population of FOR neurones, each of which is involved in a specific part of the saccade trajectory.
